hints.title: Name the two conditions
hints.body: Use one letter for primality of the displayed number and another for the condition on k. Write the given theorem as an implication.

hints.title: Compare the arrows
hints.body: Use the contrapositive rule and the meaning of sufficient to compare each translated statement with the given theorem.
hints.recap: Only the contrapositive is automatically equivalent to an implication; the converse needs separate justification.
hints.pitfall: Compare the logical forms; the statement is not asking for an experimental search through powers.
hints.pause: Determine which translations follow from the stated theorem.

recall.reminder: Only the contrapositive is automatically equivalent to an implication; the converse needs separate justification.

solution:
Let P mean “2k+1 is prime” and Q mean “k is a power of 2”. The given theorem is P⇒Q.

I asserts Q⇒P, the converse, which is not equivalent to the theorem. II says ¬P⇒¬Q; its contrapositive is also Q⇒P, so it too is not equivalent to the theorem.

III says P is sufficient for Q, precisely the given theorem. Therefore the answers are No, No, Yes: G. No separate number-theoretic proof or large-prime calculation is required.
knowledgePattern: Compare a theorem with its converse and only-if reformulation
